title: Millions could lose SNAP benefits under proposed federal rule by 2029 - ABC11 News
text:
Millions could lose SNAP benefits under proposed federal rule by 2029 - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham 
 24/7 Live Raleigh Durham Fayetteville Surrounding Area PERSONAL FINANCE 
 Proposed SNAP rule could cut benefits for millions by 2029 
 A proposed federal rule may cut SNAP benefits from 6.3 million Americans, raising concerns about food insecurity and increased demand at food banks. Department of Agriculture Food and Nutrition Administration By Penelope Lopez Wednesday, November 11, 2026 11:23PM Share FAYETTEVILLE, N.C. (WTVD) -- Millions of Americans could lose access to the nation's largest food assistance program by 2029 under a proposed rule that would restrict Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) eligibility for households receiving other forms of government assistance.
 The rule, currently under consideration, would tighten eligibility requirements for SNAP, previously known as food stamps, by ending a policy that allows states to expand access for families already enrolled in other aid programs.
 The move could especially impact local communities in the Sandhills region, including thousands of families relying on food banks.
 Elaine Williams, a SNAP recipient living on a fixed income, said the uncertainty is overwhelming.
 "It's called putting your trust in God. Because you put your trust in him anyway, but to know that's what they are thinking about doing, that makes it even worse. This is a crazy," Williams said. She spoke as she visited the Second Harvest Food Bank in Fayetteville, hoping to receive a Thanksgiving box.
 For Williams and others facing the prospect of losing benefits, the situation is dire.
 "Now is this terrible idea. I've never seen nothing like it. Food is just downright ridiculous. And, they don't even want to help anybody," she said.
 Roughly 6.3 million people, nearly one in five food stamp recipients, could lose their benefits if the rule is adopted, according to federal estimates.
 The changes would also require more paperwork for those seeking assistance and standardize eligibility across states.
 Federal SNAP spending could drop by nearly $45 billion, and state spending by $5.2 billion over five years.
 Food bank leaders are bracing for a surge in demand. "During the shutdown, we had 200 calls in the first hour of that happening. And we know that more people are going to be coming here for assistance. So, we're reaching out to our donor food donors and other partners," said David Griffin, director of Second Harvest Food Bank.
 Cumberland County currently ranks fourth in North Carolina for SNAP enrollment, with nearly 71,000 people receiving benefits in April 2025.

 Griffin says the food bank's inventory has been low for the past six to seven months, and further cuts could be devastating.
 "It's stressful to understand that you try and do all you can for a family that might come down here with a child or with a senior, and don't really know what to do. But we're going to do everything we can for them," Griffin said.
 Each month, Second Harvest Food Bank helps about 80,000 people put food on the table. With resources already stretched thin, Griffin warns the proposed cuts could have major ripple effects, particularly for children and mothers.
 The Trump administration proposed a similar rule ending "broad-based categorical eligibility" in 2019, but it was withdrawn by the Biden administration in 2021.
 The public will have 30 days to submit comments on the proposed rule.
